title: Operating Systems
summary: Discover what really happens inside your computer: the kernel, processes and threads, CPU scheduling, virtual memory, file systems, devices, concurrency and security, with hands-on C simulations of real OS algorithms.

lessons.title: What an operating system does
lessons.summary: See the OS as the manager that shares hardware between programs and gives them simple services.

slides.title: Hardware is complicated
slides.text:
A computer has:
- CPU cores
- RAM
- disks / SSDs
- keyboard, screen, network, USB...

Every device works differently. Programs should not have to care.
slides.narration: A computer is a box of very different parts: processor cores, memory, storage, a screen, a network card and much more. Each works in its own complicated way. If every program had to control the hardware directly, programming would be a nightmare.

slides.title: The OS in the middle
slides.text:
```
  Apps (browser, editor, games)
  -----------------------------
  Operating system
  -----------------------------
  Hardware (CPU, RAM, disk, devices)
```
slides.narration: The operating system sits between your programs and the hardware. Programs ask the operating system for what they need, and the operating system deals with the hardware. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are all operating systems.

slides.title: Job 1: resource manager
slides.text:
The OS **shares** hardware fairly and safely:
- CPU time between programs
- memory between processes
- disk space and devices

One crashing app should not crash the others.
slides.narration: The first job of the operating system is to be a resource manager. It shares processor time, memory and devices between all running programs, fairly and safely. It also keeps programs apart, so one crashing app does not take down the others.

slides.title: Job 2: nice abstractions
slides.text:
Hardware -> simple ideas:
- disk blocks -> **files and folders**
- CPU -> **processes and threads**
- RAM -> **virtual memory**
- network card -> **sockets**
slides.narration: The second job is to turn messy hardware into simple ideas. Disk blocks become files and folders. The processor becomes processes and threads. Memory becomes a private virtual address space for each program. The network card becomes sockets.

slides.title: You can call the OS from C
slides.text: Even `printf` ends up asking the OS to write:
slides.narration: Every program uses the operating system constantly. When this C program prints a line, the C library eventually makes a system call that asks the operating system to write bytes to the screen. You will learn more about system calls in the next lesson.

lessons.notes:
## Definition

An **operating system (OS)** is the software that manages a computer's hardware and provides common services to programs. Examples: **Windows 11**, **macOS**, **Linux** distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian), **Android** (Linux-based), **iOS**, and embedded systems like FreeRTOS.

## Two big roles

### 1. Resource manager (referee)
- **CPU**: decides which program runs on which core and for how long (scheduling).
- **Memory**: gives each process its own memory and protects it from others.
- **Storage**: organizes data into files and enforces permissions.
- **Devices**: controls printers, network cards, GPUs through **drivers**.

### 2. Extended machine (abstractions)
| Hardware | OS abstraction |
|---|---|
| CPU cores | processes, threads |
| RAM | virtual address spaces |
| disk blocks | files, directories |
| network card | sockets |
| screen, input | windows, events |

## Main parts

- **Kernel** - the core, runs with full hardware privileges.
- **System libraries** - e.g. the C library (glibc, musl, Windows CRT).
- **System programs** - shell, file manager, services/daemons.
- **User interface** - GUI desktop or command line.

## Booting in short

Firmware (UEFI) -> boot loader (GRUB, Windows Boot Manager) -> kernel -> first process (`systemd` on most Linux, `launchd` on macOS, `smss/wininit` on Windows) -> services -> login.

## Why programmers care

Understanding the OS explains why programs are slow (I/O, memory), why they crash (segmentation faults), how to run things in parallel (threads), and how to keep data safe (permissions). In this course you will also simulate several OS algorithms in C.

quiz.q: Which of these is an operating system?
quiz.explain: Linux is an OS kernel used by many distributions.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the OS is a "resource manager"?
options: It shares CPU, memory and devices between programs safely
quiz.explain: The OS allocates and protects hardware resources.

quiz.q: Which is an OS abstraction for storage?
quiz.explain: The OS turns disk blocks into files and directories.

lessons.task: Open your system's task manager (Task Manager on Windows, Activity Monitor on macOS, `top` or `htop` on Linux). Write down: how many processes are running, which uses the most CPU, which uses the most memory, and how many CPU cores you have.

lessons.title: Kernel space, user space and system calls
lessons.summary: Understand CPU privilege levels, the kernel, and how programs request services through system calls.

slides.title: Two modes
slides.text:
The CPU has privilege levels:
- **Kernel mode**: can do anything (touch any memory, any device)
- **User mode**: restricted; normal apps run here

A bug in an app cannot directly wreck the hardware.
slides.narration: Modern processors have at least two privilege levels. In kernel mode, code can do anything, including touching any memory or device. Normal applications run in user mode, where dangerous instructions are blocked. That way a buggy app cannot directly damage the system.

slides.title: System calls
slides.text:
Apps ask the kernel for help with **system calls**:
- `read`, `write`, `open`, `close`
- `fork`, `exec`, `exit` (processes)
- `mmap` (memory), `socket` (network)

A special instruction switches to kernel mode.
slides.narration: When an app needs something only the kernel can do, like reading a file, it makes a system call. A special instruction switches the processor into kernel mode, the kernel does the work after checking permissions, and then it returns to the app in user mode.

slides.title: A system call in C
slides.text: POSIX `write` sends bytes to file descriptor 1 (stdout):
slides.narration: Here we skip printf and call the write system call wrapper directly on Linux or macOS. File descriptor one is standard output. On Windows the equivalent API is called WriteFile, but the idea is the same: the program asks, the kernel acts.

slides.title: Kernel designs
slides.text:
- **Monolithic**: everything in the kernel (Linux)
- **Microkernel**: minimal kernel, services in user space (seL4, QNX, MINIX)
- **Hybrid**: mix (Windows NT, macOS XNU)
- Drivers are often **loadable modules**
slides.narration: Kernels are built in different styles. A monolithic kernel like Linux puts most services, including drivers, inside the kernel for speed. A microkernel keeps only the essentials and runs the rest as separate programs for safety. Windows and macOS use hybrid designs.

slides.title: Interrupts and exceptions
slides.text:
The kernel also runs when:
- a device signals an **interrupt** (key press, packet arrived, timer)
- a program causes an **exception** (divide by zero, bad memory access)

The timer interrupt lets the OS take the CPU back.
slides.narration: The kernel does not only run when asked. Hardware devices send interrupts, for example when a key is pressed or a network packet arrives. Programs can also trigger exceptions, like accessing invalid memory. A regular timer interrupt lets the kernel take back the processor and switch programs.

lessons.notes:
## Privilege levels

CPUs separate privileged and unprivileged execution. On x86-64 these are **rings** (ring 0 = kernel, ring 3 = user); ARM uses **exception levels** (EL1 kernel, EL0 user).

- **Kernel mode** - full access to memory, I/O, special instructions.
- **User mode** - restricted; attempts to do privileged things cause a trap.

## Kernel space vs user space

The kernel's memory is protected from user programs. Each user process gets its own address space. The kernel manages processes, memory, file systems, networking and drivers.

## System calls

A **system call** is the controlled doorway from user space into the kernel.

1. Program calls a library function (e.g. `fopen`, `printf`).
2. The library places a syscall number and arguments in registers.
3. A special instruction (`syscall` on x86-64, `svc` on ARM) switches to kernel mode.
4. The kernel validates arguments and permissions, does the work.
5. Control returns to user mode with a result or error code (`errno`).

```c
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
int fd = open("notes.txt", O_RDONLY);   // syscall
char buf[100];
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);  // syscall
close(fd);                              // syscall
```

Linux has about 450 system calls. Windows exposes the **Win32 API** (`CreateFileW`, `ReadFile`), which calls into the NT kernel. Tools like `strace` (Linux) or Process Monitor (Windows) show the calls a program makes.

## Kernel architectures

| Type | Idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Monolithic | most services inside the kernel | Linux, FreeBSD |
| Microkernel | tiny kernel, services as user processes | seL4, QNX, MINIX 3 |
| Hybrid | mostly monolithic with microkernel ideas | Windows NT, macOS XNU |

The Linux kernel is written mostly in C, and since 2022 it also accepts **Rust** code for some drivers.

## Interrupts

Devices raise **interrupts**; the CPU jumps to a kernel handler. The **timer interrupt** enables preemptive multitasking. Programs that misbehave cause **exceptions** (page fault, divide error), which the kernel handles, sometimes by killing the process (segmentation fault).

quiz.q: Why do normal apps run in user mode?
options: So bugs or malicious code cannot directly access hardware or other programs' memory
quiz.explain: User mode restricts dangerous operations.

quiz.q: What is a system call?
options: A controlled request from a program to the kernel for a service
A function in your own code
quiz.explain: Syscalls are the entry points into the kernel.

quiz.q: Which OS kernel is monolithic?
quiz.explain: Linux puts most services, including drivers, inside the kernel.

lessons.task: On Linux run `strace -c ls` (or on macOS `sudo dtruss ls` if allowed; on Windows use Process Monitor) and list the five most frequent system calls. For each, guess what `ls` used it for.

lessons.title: Processes and threads
lessons.summary: Learn what a process is, its life cycle, and how threads share work inside a process.

slides.title: Program vs process
slides.text:
- **Program**: a file on disk (`chrome.exe`, `/usr/bin/python3`)
- **Process**: a program **running**, with its own memory, open files and state

One program can run as many processes.
slides.narration: A program is just a file on disk. A process is a program that is running, with its own memory, open files and current position in the code. You can start the same program many times, and each one becomes a separate process.

slides.title: What a process has
slides.text:
- **PID** (process ID)
- Address space: code, data, **heap**, **stack**
- CPU registers, program counter
- Open files, permissions (user ID)

Stored by the kernel in a **PCB** (process control block).
slides.narration: Each process has an ID number, its own memory layout with code, data, heap and stack, its saved processor registers, and a list of open files. The kernel keeps all this in a structure called the process control block.

slides.title: Process states
slides.text:
```
new -> ready <-> running -> terminated
          ^        |
          |        v
          +---- waiting (I/O)
```
slides.narration: A process moves between states. It is created, then becomes ready to run. When the scheduler picks it, it is running. If it needs to wait for input or a disk read, it moves to waiting, then back to ready. Finally it terminates.

slides.title: Threads
slides.text:
A **thread** is a path of execution **inside** a process.

- Threads share memory, code and open files
- Each has its own stack and registers
- Cheaper to create than processes
- Can run in parallel on multiple cores
slides.narration: A thread is a separate path of execution inside a process. All threads in a process share the same memory and files, but each has its own stack and registers. Threads are cheaper than processes and can run in parallel on several cores.

slides.title: Threads in C (POSIX)
slides.text: Two threads running at once:
slides.narration: Here is a small example with POSIX threads. The main thread starts a worker with pthread create, and then waits for it with pthread join. On Linux and macOS you compile with the dash pthread flag. Windows has its own thread API, and C eleven also defines portable threads.

slides.title: Process or thread?
slides.text:
- **Processes**: strong isolation (a crash stays contained). Example: browser tabs
- **Threads**: fast sharing of data. Example: a game engine's render and physics threads
- Shared memory needs **synchronization** (later lesson)
slides.narration: When should you use each? Processes give strong isolation: modern browsers run tabs in separate processes so one crash does not kill the rest. Threads share data cheaply, which suits work like a game engine. But shared memory must be protected, which we will cover in the concurrency lesson.

lessons.notes:
## Process

A **process** is an instance of a running program. The kernel tracks each one in a **Process Control Block (PCB)** containing:
- PID and parent PID
- state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated)
- saved registers and program counter
- memory map, open file descriptors
- owner (user ID), priority, accounting info

## Memory layout

```
high addresses  +-----------+
                |  stack    |  local variables, grows down
                |    ...    |
                |  heap     |  malloc/new, grows up
                |  data/bss |  global variables
low addresses   |  text     |  machine code
                +-----------+
```

## Creating processes

- **POSIX**: `fork()` copies the current process, `exec()` replaces it with a new program, `wait()` waits for a child.
- **Windows**: `CreateProcess()` does both in one step.

## Context switch

When the OS switches CPUs from one process to another it saves registers into the PCB and loads the next one's. This takes microseconds, so too many switches waste time.

## Threads

A **thread** is the unit the scheduler runs. A process has one or more threads which share code, heap, globals and files, but each thread has its own **stack**, **registers** and **thread ID**.

| | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | separate | shared |
| Creation cost | higher | lower |
| Crash impact | isolated | can kill whole process |
| Communication | pipes, sockets, shared memory | direct variables (with locks) |

```c
// compile: gcc main.c -pthread
pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, NULL);
pthread_join(t, NULL);
```

C11 also provides `<threads.h>` (`thrd_create`, `mtx_lock`), and many languages offer higher-level tools: thread pools, async/await, goroutines, virtual threads (Java 21+).

## Concurrency vs parallelism

- **Concurrency**: several tasks in progress, maybe taking turns on one core.
- **Parallelism**: tasks literally running at the same time on several cores.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is a file; a process is a running instance of it
A process is a file; a program is running
A program has threads, a process does not
quiz.explain: Processes are programs in execution.

quiz.q: What do threads of the same process share?
options: The heap, globals and open files
quiz.explain: Threads share memory and files but have their own stacks and registers.

quiz.q: A process is waiting for a disk read. Which state is it in?
quiz.explain: Processes waiting for I/O are in the waiting/blocked state.

lessons.task: Using Task Manager (Details tab, add the Threads column), Activity Monitor, or `ps -eLf | wc -l` and `top -H` on Linux, find a program with many threads (a browser is a good candidate). Note its number of processes and threads, and explain why it might use so many.

lessons.title: CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF and priorities
lessons.summary: Learn how the OS decides which process runs next, and simulate First-Come First-Served in C.

slides.title: Why schedule?
slides.text:
More threads than cores.

The **scheduler** picks who runs next. Goals:
- high CPU **utilization**
- low **waiting** and **turnaround** time
- fast **response** for interactive apps
- **fairness**
slides.narration: Your computer runs far more threads than it has cores, so something must decide who runs next. That is the scheduler. It tries to keep the processor busy, finish jobs quickly, respond fast to the user, and be fair to everyone.

slides.title: Key measures
slides.text:
- **Burst time**: CPU time a process needs
- **Turnaround** = finish - arrival
- **Waiting** = turnaround - burst
- **Response** = first run - arrival
slides.narration: To compare algorithms we use a few measures. Burst time is how much processor time a job needs. Turnaround time is finish time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround minus burst, the time spent waiting in the queue. Response time is how long until the job first runs.

slides.title: FCFS: First-Come, First-Served
slides.text:
Run jobs in arrival order, each to completion.

P1=24, P2=3, P3=3 (all at time 0):

`| P1 0-24 | P2 24-27 | P3 27-30 |`

Waiting: 0, 24, 27 -> average **17**
slides.narration: The simplest algorithm is first come, first served. Jobs run in the order they arrive, each until it is finished. With one long job of twenty four and two short jobs of three, the short jobs wait a long time, giving an average waiting time of seventeen.

slides.title: The convoy effect
slides.text:
Same jobs, short ones first:

`| P2 0-3 | P3 3-6 | P1 6-30 |`

Waiting: 6, 0, 3 -> average **3**

Short jobs stuck behind a long one = **convoy effect**.
slides.narration: If the short jobs had come first, the average waiting time would be only three. When short jobs get stuck behind a long one, we call it the convoy effect. This is the main weakness of first come, first served.

slides.title: SJF and priorities
slides.text:
- **SJF** (Shortest Job First): pick the smallest burst; optimal average waiting, but needs to know burst lengths; long jobs may **starve**
- **SRTF**: preemptive SJF
- **Priority**: highest priority first; fix starvation with **aging**
slides.narration: Shortest job first always picks the smallest job. It gives the best possible average waiting time, but the OS cannot know burst lengths exactly, and long jobs might starve. Priority scheduling runs the most important work first, and aging slowly raises the priority of jobs that have waited long.

slides.title: Real schedulers
slides.text:
- **Linux**: EEVDF scheduler (since kernel 6.6), replaced CFS
- **Windows**: priority-based, preemptive, 32 levels
- **macOS**: priority bands + QoS classes
- All are **preemptive** and multi-core aware
slides.narration: Real operating systems use much more advanced schedulers. Linux uses EEVDF since version six point six, which aims to give each task a fair share with low latency. Windows uses thirty two priority levels. All modern schedulers are preemptive and spread work across many cores.

lessons.notes:
## Scheduling criteria

- **CPU utilization** - keep cores busy.
- **Throughput** - jobs finished per unit of time.
- **Turnaround time** = completion - arrival.
- **Waiting time** = turnaround - burst.
- **Response time** = first run - arrival (important for interactive apps).

## Preemptive vs non-preemptive

- **Non-preemptive**: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks.
- **Preemptive**: the OS can interrupt it (timer interrupt). All modern desktop/server OSes are preemptive.

## Algorithms

| Algorithm | Rule | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| FCFS | arrival order | simple, fair order | convoy effect |
| SJF | shortest burst first | minimal average waiting | needs burst estimate, starvation |
| SRTF | preemptive SJF | even better average | more switches, starvation |
| Priority | highest priority first | expresses importance | starvation (fix: aging) |
| Round Robin | time slices in turn | good response | next lesson |
| Multilevel feedback queue | several queues, jobs move between | adapts to behavior | complex to tune |

## FCFS worked example

Processes `(arrival, burst)`: P1 (0,5), P2 (1,3), P3 (2,8), P4 (3,6).

```
| P1 0-5 | P2 5-8 | P3 8-16 | P4 16-22 |
```

| P | finish | turnaround | waiting |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| P2 | 8 | 7 | 4 |
| P3 | 16 | 14 | 6 |
| P4 | 22 | 19 | 13 |

Average waiting = 23/4 = 5.75. If the CPU is free before the next process arrives, it sits **idle** until that arrival.

## Real systems

Linux replaced CFS with **EEVDF** (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) in kernel 6.6 (2023). Windows uses preemptive priority scheduling with dynamic boosts. Mobile OSes also schedule for energy, using performance and efficiency cores.

quiz.q: Turnaround time is...
quiz.explain: Turnaround measures total time in the system.

quiz.q: What is the convoy effect?
options: Short jobs waiting behind a long job under FCFS
quiz.explain: FCFS can make many short jobs wait for one long one.

quiz.q: Which technique fixes starvation in priority scheduling?
quiz.explain: Aging gradually raises the priority of waiting jobs.

lessons.title: Round-robin and time slicing
lessons.summary: Share the CPU in turns with a time quantum, and simulate round-robin scheduling in C.

slides.title: Taking turns
slides.text:
**Round robin (RR)**: every ready process gets a small **time quantum** (e.g. 4 ms), then goes to the back of the queue.

- Preemptive (timer interrupt)
- Nobody waits forever
- Great for interactive systems
slides.narration: Round robin is like children taking turns on a swing. Each ready process gets a small slice of time called a quantum. When its time is up, the timer interrupt stops it, and it goes to the back of the queue. Nobody waits forever, which makes it great for interactive systems.

slides.title: Example, quantum = 4
slides.narration: With a quantum of four, P1 runs for four units, then P2 runs its three units and finishes, then P3 finishes too. P1 then gets the rest of the time. The average waiting time is about five point six seven, much better than first come first served for this set.

slides.title: Choosing the quantum
slides.text:
- **Too large** -> behaves like FCFS
- **Too small** -> too many context switches (overhead)
- Rule of thumb: most CPU bursts should finish within one quantum
- Typical: a few milliseconds
slides.narration: Choosing the quantum is a balancing act. If it is very large, round robin becomes first come first served. If it is very small, the system wastes time switching between processes. A good quantum lets most short bursts finish in one turn, typically a few milliseconds.

slides.title: The ready queue in code
slides.text: A simple array queue is enough:
slides.narration: In a simulation you can implement the ready queue with an array and two indexes, head and tail. Take a process from the head, run it for one quantum or less, and if it still has work left, add it at the tail. Repeat until the queue is empty.

slides.title: Beyond plain RR
slides.text:
- **Multilevel feedback queues**: interactive jobs stay high priority, CPU-heavy jobs sink
- Used in some form by Windows, macOS, older Linux
- Modern Linux EEVDF also uses time slices with virtual deadlines
slides.narration: Real systems combine round robin with priorities. Multilevel feedback queues keep interactive tasks at high priority, while long running number crunchers drift lower. Linux's EEVDF scheduler also hands out time slices, but chooses who runs next using virtual deadlines.

lessons.notes:
## Round Robin (RR)

Each process in the ready queue gets at most one **time quantum** `q` of CPU, then is preempted and placed at the back. With `n` processes, no process waits more than `(n-1) x q` before its next turn.

## Worked example

`q = 2`, bursts P1=5, P2=3, P3=1, P4=4 (all arrive at 0).

```
| P1 0-2 | P2 2-4 | P3 4-5 | P4 5-7 | P1 7-9 | P2 9-10 | P4 10-12 | P1 12-13 |
```

| P | finish | waiting = finish - burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 13 | 8 |
| P2 | 10 | 7 |
| P3 | 5 | 4 |
| P4 | 12 | 8 |

Completion order: P3, P2, P4, P1. Average waiting = 27/4 = 6.75.

(When every process arrives at time 0, turnaround = finish time.)

## Quantum size

- Large quantum -> fewer switches, worse response, approaches FCFS.
- Small quantum -> great response, but context-switch overhead grows.
- Typical quanta are a few milliseconds; context switches cost microseconds.

## Properties

- Fair and starvation-free.
- Average waiting time is often higher than SJF, but **response time** is much better.
- Works well with mixed I/O-bound and CPU-bound workloads.

## Multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)

Several RR queues with different priorities and quanta. New jobs start high; if a job uses its whole quantum it moves down; if it gives up the CPU early (I/O, interactive) it stays up. Periodically everything is boosted to avoid starvation.

## Implementation tip

A queue can be an array with `head` and `tail` indexes, or a circular buffer of size `n` because each process appears at most once in the queue at any moment.

quiz.q: What happens when a process uses up its quantum in RR?
options: It is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue
quiz.explain: RR preempts and requeues it.

quiz.q: What happens if the quantum is very large?
quiz.explain: With a huge quantum, each job finishes in one turn, like FCFS.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of a very small quantum?
quiz.explain: Each switch costs time that does no useful work.

exercise.title: Simulate round-robin scheduling
exercise.prompt:
Simulate **Round Robin** scheduling where all processes arrive at time 0.

**Input**: `n q` (number of processes, time quantum), then `n` burst times. Processes are `P1`..`Pn`; the ready queue starts in that order.

**Rules**: take the process at the front of the queue and run it for `min(q, remaining)` time units. If it still has time left, put it at the back of the queue. Context switches take no time.

**Output**:
1. `Order:` followed by the processes in the order they finish, e.g. `Order: P2 P3 P1`
2. For each process in **index order**: `P<i> waiting=<w> turnaround=<t>` (turnaround = finish time, waiting = turnaround - burst)
3. `Average waiting=<x>` with 2 decimals

Example input:
```
3 4
24 3 3
```
Output:
```
Order: P2 P3 P1
P1 waiting=6 turnaround=30
P2 waiting=4 turnaround=7
P3 waiting=7 turnaround=10
Average waiting=5.67
```

Order: P2 P3 P4 P5 P1
P1 waiting=9 turnaround=19
P2 waiting=3 turnaround=4
P3 waiting=4 turnaround=6
P4 waiting=6 turnaround=7
P5 waiting=10 turnaround=15
Average waiting=6.40

lessons.title: Memory management and virtual memory
lessons.summary: Learn how each process gets its own address space, and how paging and the MMU make it work.

slides.title: The problem
slides.text:
Many processes, one RAM.
- Keep them **apart** (protection)
- Let each believe it has a big, clean memory
- Use RAM efficiently
- Run programs bigger than free RAM
slides.narration: Many processes share one physical memory. The OS must keep them apart, give each one the illusion of a large clean memory space, use RAM efficiently, and even run programs that need more memory than is currently free.

slides.title: Virtual addresses
slides.text:
Programs use **virtual addresses**.

The **MMU** (memory management unit) in the CPU translates each one to a **physical address** using the OS's **page tables**.

Same virtual address in two processes -> different physical RAM.
slides.narration: Programs never see real memory addresses. They use virtual addresses, and a hardware unit in the processor, the MMU, translates each one into a physical address using tables set up by the OS. Two processes can use the same virtual address and still touch completely different physical memory.

slides.title: Paging
slides.text:
Memory is split into fixed-size blocks:
- virtual **pages**, physical **frames** (commonly 4 KiB)
- page table: page number -> frame number
- **TLB**: a small cache of recent translations
slides.narration: The most common technique is paging. Virtual memory is cut into pages, and physical memory into frames of the same size, usually four kilobytes. The page table records which frame holds each page. A small fast cache called the TLB remembers recent translations.

slides.title: Page faults and swapping
slides.text:
Page not in RAM? -> **page fault**
1. OS finds a free frame (or evicts one)
2. Loads the page from disk (swap / file)
3. Updates page table, restarts the instruction

Too much of this = **thrashing**.
slides.narration: If a program touches a page that is not in RAM, the hardware raises a page fault. The OS finds a free frame, possibly evicting another page, loads the needed page from disk, and restarts the instruction. When this happens constantly, the system slows to a crawl, which is called thrashing.

slides.title: Seeing addresses in C
slides.text: Every process sees its own virtual addresses:
slides.narration: This program prints the virtual addresses of a global variable, a heap block and a local variable. Run it twice and the numbers often change, because of a security feature called address space layout randomization. These are virtual addresses, not physical ones.

slides.title: Benefits
slides.text:
- **Isolation**: a process cannot see another's memory
- **Sharing**: libraries mapped once, used by many
- **Copy-on-write**: fast `fork`
- **Overcommit**: bigger than RAM via swap
- **ASLR**: random layout against attacks
slides.narration: Virtual memory brings many benefits. Processes are isolated from each other. Shared libraries can be loaded once and mapped into many processes. Fork can be fast thanks to copy on write. Programs can use more memory than is physically free, and random layouts make attacks harder.

lessons.notes:
## Goals of memory management

- **Protection** - processes cannot read or write each other's memory.
- **Abstraction** - each process sees a large, contiguous address space.
- **Efficiency** - share RAM well, load only what is needed.

## Virtual memory and the MMU

Every memory access uses a **virtual address**. The CPU's **MMU** translates it to a **physical address** using **page tables** managed by the kernel. On x86-64 and ARM64 these are multi-level tables (4 or 5 levels).

## Paging

- Virtual memory is divided into **pages**, physical memory into **frames** (typically 4 KiB; "huge pages" of 2 MiB or 1 GiB also exist; Apple Silicon uses 16 KiB).
- Address = page number + offset. Example with 4 KiB pages: virtual address 8200 = page 2, offset 8.
- Each page-table entry stores the frame number plus bits: present, writable, user-accessible, dirty, accessed, no-execute.
- The **TLB** caches recent translations; a TLB miss costs a page-table walk.

## Page faults

A **page fault** happens when a page is not present (or access is not allowed):
1. Trap to the kernel.
2. If the access is invalid -> segmentation fault (process killed).
3. Otherwise find a free frame; if none, choose a **victim** page (page replacement, next lesson), writing it to disk if dirty.
4. Read the page from swap or the file, update the table, resume.

**Demand paging** loads pages only when first used. **Thrashing** occurs when the working set of all processes does not fit in RAM.

## Other techniques

- **Copy-on-write**: after `fork`, parent and child share pages until one writes.
- **Memory-mapped files** (`mmap`): files appear as memory.
- **Shared libraries**: one physical copy, many mappings.
- **ASLR**: randomized layout to resist exploits.
- **Memory compression**: macOS, Windows and Linux (zram/zswap) compress pages before swapping.

## Fragmentation

- **External** fragmentation (free memory in small scattered pieces) is avoided by paging.
- **Internal** fragmentation: unused space inside the last page of an allocation.

quiz.q: What does the MMU do?
options: Translates virtual addresses to physical addresses
quiz.explain: The memory management unit performs address translation.

quiz.q: With 4 KiB (4096-byte) pages, which page contains virtual address 8200?
quiz.explain: 8200 / 4096 = 2 remainder 8, so page 2, offset 8.

quiz.q: What is thrashing?
options: The system spending most of its time handling page faults instead of useful work
quiz.explain: When the working set exceeds RAM, constant paging kills performance.

lessons.task: Open your task manager or run `free -h` (Linux) / `vm_stat` (macOS) / Task Manager Performance tab (Windows). Record total RAM, used RAM, and swap/page file usage. Then open many browser tabs and see how the numbers change.

lessons.title: Page replacement: FIFO and LRU
lessons.summary: Decide which page to evict when memory is full, and count hits and faults in C.

slides.title: Memory is full
slides.text:
A page fault needs a frame, but all frames are used.

Which page do we **evict**?

Goal: **fewest page faults**.
slides.narration: When a page fault happens and every frame is already in use, the OS must pick a victim page to remove. A good choice means few future page faults. A bad choice means the page we just removed is needed again right away.

slides.title: FIFO
slides.text:
Evict the page that was **loaded first**.

Frames=3, refs `7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 ...`

- Simple: a queue
- But old pages may be hot (heavily used)!
slides.narration: First in, first out evicts the page that has been in memory the longest. It is easy to implement with a queue. But the oldest page might be one that is used all the time, so FIFO often makes poor choices.

slides.title: Belady's anomaly
slides.text:
With FIFO, **more frames can cause more faults**!

Refs: `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`
- 3 frames -> 9 faults
- 4 frames -> 10 faults
slides.narration: FIFO has a strange weakness called Belady's anomaly. For some reference strings, giving it more memory actually causes more page faults. With this famous string, three frames give nine faults, but four frames give ten.

slides.title: LRU and Optimal
slides.text:
- **OPT** (Belady): evict the page used **furthest in the future**. Best possible, but needs the future.
- **LRU**: evict the page **least recently used**. Uses the past to guess the future. No Belady anomaly.
slides.narration: The optimal algorithm evicts the page that will not be needed for the longest time. It is perfect but impossible in practice, since it needs to know the future. Least recently used approximates it by looking at the past: the page untouched for the longest time is evicted. LRU never suffers from Belady's anomaly.

slides.title: Simulating with an array
slides.text: Keep pages so `mem[0]` is always the next victim:
slides.narration: A simple simulation keeps the pages in an array where the first element is always the next victim. On a fault, remove the first element and add the new page at the end. For LRU, also move a page to the end every time it is used. For FIFO, a hit changes nothing.

slides.title: Real systems: approximations
slides.text:
Exact LRU is too costly in hardware.

- **Clock / second chance**: uses the "accessed" bit
- Linux: active/inactive lists, **multi-gen LRU** (MGLRU)
- Windows: working sets + standby list
slides.narration: Tracking exact LRU for every memory access would be far too slow. Real systems approximate it. The clock algorithm uses the hardware accessed bit to give pages a second chance. Linux uses multi generational LRU lists, and Windows manages working sets for each process.

lessons.notes:
## The replacement problem

On a page fault with no free frame, choose a **victim**. Measure algorithms by number of **faults** (or **hit ratio** = hits / references) on a **reference string**.

## FIFO

Evict the oldest loaded page.

Reference string `7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1`, 3 frames:
- FIFO: **15 faults**, 5 hits.
- LRU: **12 faults**, 8 hits.
- OPT: 9 faults.

## Belady's anomaly

FIFO with `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`:
- 3 frames: 9 faults
- 4 frames: 10 faults

More memory, more faults! **Stack algorithms** like LRU and OPT never show this.

## LRU

Evict the page whose last use is the oldest. It works because programs have **locality**: recently used pages tend to be used again soon.

Implementations: timestamp per page, or a list where a used page moves to the front.

## OPT (optimal)

Evict the page whose next use is furthest away. Not implementable online, but a useful benchmark.

## Approximations in real OSes

- **Clock (second chance)**: frames in a circle; a hand skips pages with the accessed bit set (clearing it) and evicts the first page with bit 0.
- **Dirty bit**: prefer evicting clean pages (no write-back needed).
- **Linux**: active/inactive lists and the **multi-generational LRU** (MGLRU, merged in kernel 6.1).

## Simulation tip

```c
// mem[0] is always the next victim
// FIFO: hit -> nothing; fault -> remove mem[0] if full, append page
// LRU : hit -> move page to end; fault -> same as FIFO
```

The same simple structure works for both algorithms; only the hit rule differs.

quiz.q: Which page does FIFO evict?
options: The one loaded into memory first
The one used furthest in the future
quiz.explain: FIFO removes the oldest loaded page.

quiz.q: What is Belady's anomaly?
options: FIFO producing more faults with more frames
quiz.explain: With FIFO, adding frames can increase faults for some strings.

quiz.q: Why is OPT not used in real systems?
options: It is too slow to compile
It needs to know future page references
quiz.explain: OPT requires knowledge of the future.

exercise.title: Count page hits: FIFO and LRU
exercise.prompt:
Simulate page replacement.

**Input**:
- line 1: number of frames `f` (1 to 100) and the algorithm name `FIFO` or `LRU`
- line 2: `n`, the number of page references (up to 1000)
- line 3: `n` page numbers

Memory starts empty. A reference to a page already in memory is a **hit**; otherwise it is a **fault** and the page is loaded (evicting a page if all `f` frames are full).
- **FIFO** evicts the page that was loaded earliest.
- **LRU** evicts the page whose most recent use is the oldest.

**Output** exactly two lines:
```
Hits: <h>
Faults: <f>
```

Example input:
```
3 FIFO
12
1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5
```
Output:
```
Hits: 3
Faults: 9
```

lessons.title: File systems
lessons.summary: Learn how files and folders are stored on disk, and the file systems used by Windows, macOS and Linux.

slides.title: From blocks to files
slides.text:
A disk is just numbered **blocks** (e.g. 4 KiB).

The **file system** gives you:
- files with names
- folders (directories)
- metadata: size, dates, owner, permissions
slides.narration: A disk or SSD is basically a long list of numbered blocks. A file system organizes those blocks into named files and folders, and keeps metadata like the size, the dates and who owns each file.

slides.title: Inodes and directories (Unix)
slides.text:
- **inode**: file metadata + pointers to data blocks
- **directory**: a list of `name -> inode number`
- **hard link**: two names, one inode
- **symbolic link**: a file containing a path
slides.narration: In Unix style file systems, each file is described by an inode, which stores metadata and the locations of the data blocks. A directory is simply a list that maps names to inode numbers. A hard link is a second name for the same inode, while a symbolic link is a small file that contains a path.

slides.title: Common file systems
slides.text:
| OS | File system |
|---|---|
| Windows | **NTFS** (also ReFS, exFAT) |
| macOS / iOS | **APFS** |
| Linux | **ext4**, Btrfs, XFS |
| USB drives | **exFAT**, FAT32 |
slides.narration: Each operating system has its favorites. Windows uses NTFS. Apple devices use APFS. Linux most often uses ext4, with Btrfs and XFS also popular. For USB sticks that must work everywhere, exFAT is the usual choice.

slides.title: Surviving crashes
slides.text:
Power cut in the middle of a write?

- **Journaling** (NTFS, ext4): write intent to a log first, replay after crash
- **Copy-on-write** (APFS, Btrfs, ZFS): never overwrite; write new blocks then switch pointers
- Enables **snapshots**
slides.narration: What if the power fails in the middle of saving? Journaling file systems first write what they plan to do into a log, so they can finish or undo it after a crash. Copy on write file systems never overwrite data in place; they write new blocks and then switch a pointer, which also makes cheap snapshots possible.

slides.title: Files from C
slides.text: The OS gives you a simple API:
slides.narration: From a program, files feel simple. You open a file, write or read bytes, and close it. Underneath, the C library makes system calls, and the kernel's file system code finds the right blocks on the disk.

slides.title: Paths and mounting
slides.text:
- Windows: drive letters `C:\Users\ana\file.txt`
- Linux/macOS: one tree from `/`, other disks **mounted** into it (`/mnt/usb`, `/Volumes/USB`)
- Separators: `\` vs `/`
slides.narration: Paths look different across systems. Windows uses drive letters and backslashes. Linux and macOS have a single tree that starts at slash, and other disks are mounted as folders inside it. Writing code that handles both separators makes your programs portable.

lessons.notes:
## What a file system does

A **file system** maps names to data on a block device and stores **metadata**: size, timestamps, owner, permissions. It also manages free space and tries to stay consistent after crashes.

## Unix model

- **Inode** - holds metadata and block pointers (direct, indirect, or **extents** in ext4).
- **Directory** - a special file mapping names to inode numbers.
- **Hard link** - another directory entry for the same inode (`ln a b`).
- **Symbolic link** - a small file containing a path (`ln -s target link`).
- Everything is a file: devices appear under `/dev`, kernel info under `/proc` and `/sys`.

```bash
ls -li          # show inode numbers
stat notes.txt  # full metadata
df -h           # free space per file system
```

## Popular file systems

| Name | Used by | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NTFS | Windows | journaling, ACLs, compression |
| ReFS | Windows Server, Dev Drive | resilient, copy-on-write features |
| APFS | macOS, iOS | copy-on-write, snapshots, encryption, SSD-optimized |
| ext4 | Linux default on many distros | journaling, extents |
| Btrfs | Fedora default, openSUSE | copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums |
| XFS | RHEL default | high-performance, large files |
| ZFS | servers, NAS | pooled storage, checksums, snapshots |
| exFAT / FAT32 | USB, SD cards | portable, no permissions; FAT32 max file 4 GiB |

## Consistency

- **Journaling**: metadata (sometimes data) changes go to a journal first; after a crash the journal is replayed.
- **Copy-on-write**: new versions are written elsewhere, then a root pointer switches atomically. Enables snapshots and checksums.

## Caching

The OS keeps file data in the **page cache** and writes later. `fflush` empties C's buffer; `fsync()` asks the OS to push data to the device. Databases rely on `fsync` for durability.

## Paths

- Windows: `C:\Users\ana\notes.txt` (also accepts `/` in most APIs).
- Unix: `/home/ana/notes.txt`; other devices are **mounted** into the tree.

quiz.q: In Unix file systems, what does a directory store?
options: A mapping from names to inode numbers
quiz.explain: Directories map names to inodes.

quiz.q: Which file system is the default on modern macOS?
quiz.explain: Apple File System has been the default since 2017.

quiz.q: How does journaling help?
options: Lets the file system recover a consistent state after a crash
quiz.explain: The journal records intended changes for replay after crashes.

lessons.task: On your computer, find which file system each drive uses (Windows: Disk Management or `fsutil fsinfo volumeinfo C:`; macOS: `diskutil info /`; Linux: `df -T`). Then create a file, a hard link and a symbolic link (`mklink` / `mklink /H` on Windows, `ln` / `ln -s` elsewhere), delete the original, and explain which links still work.

lessons.title: I/O, devices and drivers
lessons.summary: See how the OS talks to keyboards, disks, GPUs and network cards.

slides.title: Many kinds of devices
slides.text:
- **Block devices**: disks, SSDs (fixed-size blocks)
- **Character devices**: keyboard, serial ports (streams)
- **Network devices**: packets

Speeds range from bytes/second to many GB/second.
slides.narration: Computers talk to many kinds of devices. Block devices like SSDs store data in fixed size blocks. Character devices like keyboards send streams of bytes. Network devices send and receive packets. Their speeds differ by a factor of billions.

slides.title: Device drivers
slides.text:
A **driver** is code that knows one device.

- Translates OS requests to device commands
- Usually runs in the kernel
- Buggy drivers are a top cause of crashes (blue screens)
slides.narration: A device driver is the code that knows how to control one specific device. It translates generic requests from the OS into the commands that device understands. Drivers usually run inside the kernel, so a buggy driver can crash the whole system.

slides.title: Polling vs interrupts vs DMA
slides.text:
- **Polling**: CPU keeps asking "done yet?" (wastes CPU)
- **Interrupts**: device signals when ready
- **DMA**: device copies data to RAM **by itself**, then interrupts

Modern NVMe and network cards use DMA + interrupts.
slides.narration: There are three ways to wait for a device. With polling, the processor keeps asking if the device is ready, which wastes time. With interrupts, the device signals when it is done. With direct memory access, the device copies data into memory by itself and only interrupts at the end. Fast devices use DMA.

slides.title: Buffering and caching
slides.text:
- **Buffer**: holds data between fast and slow parts
- **Cache**: keeps copies to avoid slow reads
- **Spooling**: queue jobs for a device (printing)

That is why `printf` output may appear later!
slides.narration: The OS smooths over speed differences with buffers and caches. A buffer holds data moving between fast and slow parts. A cache keeps copies of data to avoid reading it again. That is why output from printf can appear later than you expect: it is waiting in a buffer.

slides.title: Buffered output in C
slides.text: Standard output is buffered:
slides.narration: Here you can see buffering. Standard output is often line buffered on a terminal and fully buffered when redirected to a file. Calling fflush forces the buffer out immediately, which is helpful when you print progress messages.

slides.title: Disk scheduling (HDDs)
slides.text:
Spinning disks: moving the head is slow.
- **FCFS**, **SSTF** (shortest seek), **SCAN** (elevator)

SSDs have no head: Linux often uses `none` or `mq-deadline` for NVMe.
slides.narration: For old spinning hard drives, moving the read head is slow, so the OS reorders requests. The elevator algorithm sweeps back and forth like a lift. Modern SSDs have no moving parts, so these tricks matter much less, and Linux often uses a very simple scheduler for them.

lessons.notes:
## Device types

| Type | Access | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Block | random access to fixed-size blocks | HDD, SSD, NVMe, USB stick |
| Character | stream of bytes | keyboard, mouse, serial port, terminal |
| Network | packets via sockets | Ethernet, Wi-Fi |

On Linux, devices appear as files in `/dev` (`/dev/nvme0n1`, `/dev/tty`). Windows uses device objects and names like `\\.\PhysicalDrive0`.

## Device drivers

A **driver** knows the registers and protocol of a device and offers a standard interface to the kernel. On Linux, drivers are often **loadable kernel modules** (`lsmod`, `modprobe`). Windows drivers use the WDF framework and must be signed. Some drivers run in user space for safety (e.g. many USB and printer drivers).

## How data moves

1. **Programmed I/O / polling** - CPU repeatedly checks a status register.
2. **Interrupt-driven I/O** - device raises an interrupt when ready.
3. **DMA** - device transfers blocks directly to/from RAM; CPU is free until the completion interrupt.

Modern high-speed devices (NVMe SSDs, 100 Gb network cards) use many **queues**, DMA and interrupt moderation. Linux's **io_uring** lets programs submit many I/O requests with few system calls.

## Buffering, caching, spooling

- **Buffering** smooths speed mismatches; C's `stdout` is line-buffered on terminals and fully buffered when redirected. Use `fflush(stdout)` when needed.
- **Caching**: the page cache keeps recently used file data in RAM.
- **Spooling**: print jobs queue on disk until the printer is ready.

## Blocking vs non-blocking I/O

- **Blocking**: the thread waits (state = waiting) until data arrives.
- **Non-blocking / async**: the call returns immediately; the program is notified later (`epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows). Node.js, nginx and async frameworks are built on these.

## Disk scheduling

For HDDs: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN (elevator), C-SCAN reduce head movement. For SSDs: minimal scheduling (`none`, `mq-deadline`, `kyber`, `bfq` on Linux).

quiz.q: What is DMA?
options: Devices copying data to/from RAM without the CPU moving every byte
quiz.explain: Direct Memory Access frees the CPU during transfers.

quiz.q: Why can a buggy driver crash the whole computer?
options: Drivers usually run in kernel mode with full privileges
They are downloaded from the internet
quiz.explain: Kernel-mode code can corrupt the whole system.

quiz.q: Why might text printed without a newline not appear right away?
options: stdout is buffered; fflush forces it out
quiz.explain: Buffered output waits until the buffer is flushed.

lessons.task: List the devices on your computer (Windows: Device Manager; macOS: System Information; Linux: `lsblk`, `lsusb`, `lspci`). Pick three and find the name of the driver each uses (Linux: `lspci -k`). Classify each as block, character or network.

lessons.title: Concurrency, race conditions and deadlocks
lessons.summary: Protect shared data with locks, understand deadlocks, and check safe states with the Banker's algorithm in C.

slides.title: Race conditions
slides.text:
Two threads run `count++` 1,000,000 times each.

Expected: 2,000,000. Got: **1,374,219**?!

`count++` = load, add, store. Threads interleave and **lose updates**.
slides.narration: When threads share data, strange bugs appear. Two threads each add one to a counter a million times, but the result is less than two million. That is because count plus plus is really three steps: load, add and store. If threads interleave those steps, updates get lost. This is a race condition.

slides.title: Mutual exclusion
slides.text: Protect the **critical section** with a **mutex**:
slides.narration: The fix is to make the critical section, the code that touches shared data, run by only one thread at a time. A mutex is a lock: a thread locks it before the critical section and unlocks it afterwards. Other threads wait their turn.

slides.title: Other tools
slides.text:
- **Semaphore**: a counter for N resources
- **Condition variable**: wait until something is true
- **Atomic operations**: `atomic_fetch_add` (C11 `<stdatomic.h>`)
- **Read-write locks**: many readers or one writer
slides.narration: There are other synchronization tools. A semaphore is a counter that allows up to N threads in. Condition variables let a thread sleep until a condition becomes true. Atomic operations update a single variable safely without a lock. Read write locks allow many readers or one writer.

slides.title: Deadlock
slides.text:
Thread A holds lock 1, wants lock 2.
Thread B holds lock 2, wants lock 1.

Both wait **forever**.

Four conditions (Coffman): **mutual exclusion**, **hold and wait**, **no preemption**, **circular wait**.
slides.narration: Locks bring a new danger: deadlock. Thread A holds lock one and waits for lock two, while thread B holds lock two and waits for lock one. Both wait forever. A deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait.

slides.title: Handling deadlocks
slides.text:
- **Prevent**: break a condition, e.g. always take locks in the **same global order**
- **Avoid**: grant requests only if the system stays in a **safe state** (Banker's algorithm)
- **Detect and recover**: find cycles, kill or roll back
- **Ignore**: most desktop OSes (reboot!)
slides.narration: There are four strategies. Prevention breaks one of the four conditions, most often by always taking locks in the same order. Avoidance only grants requests that keep the system in a safe state, using the Banker's algorithm. Detection finds cycles and recovers. And many desktop systems simply ignore the problem.

slides.title: Banker's algorithm
slides.text:
- **Need = Max - Allocation**
- Work = Available
- Find a process with Need <= Work; pretend it finishes: Work += its Allocation
- Repeat. All finish -> **SAFE** (with a safe sequence). Stuck -> **UNSAFE**
slides.narration: The Banker's algorithm checks if a state is safe. For each process, need equals its maximum claim minus what it already holds. Start with work equal to the available resources. Find a process whose need fits in work, pretend it finishes and returns its resources, and repeat. If every process can finish, the state is safe.

lessons.notes:
## Race conditions

A **race condition** occurs when the result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data. `count++` compiles to load-add-store; interleavings lose updates.

## Critical sections and locks

Code that touches shared data is a **critical section**. Requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting.

```c
pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
balance += amount;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
```

Tools: **mutexes**, **semaphores** (`sem_wait`/`sem_post`), **condition variables**, **read-write locks**, **atomics** (`<stdatomic.h>`), and higher-level channels or message passing.

Classic problems: producer-consumer (bounded buffer), readers-writers, dining philosophers.

## Deadlock

A set of threads each waiting for a resource held by another. **Coffman conditions** (all four needed):
1. Mutual exclusion
2. Hold and wait
3. No preemption
4. Circular wait

## Strategies

- **Prevention** - break a condition. Most practical: a **global lock order** (always lock A before B).
- **Avoidance** - Banker's algorithm (Dijkstra): only grant a request if the resulting state is **safe**.
- **Detection and recovery** - build a wait-for graph, find cycles, abort or roll back a victim. Databases do this.
- **Ostrich** - ignore it; most general-purpose OSes leave it to programmers.

## Banker's safety check

```
Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j]
Work = Available; Finish[i] = false
repeat:
    find i with Finish[i] == false and Need[i] <= Work
    Work += Allocation[i]; Finish[i] = true
until no such i
safe if all Finish[i] are true
```

Classic example: Available = (3,3,2), 5 processes. Scanning from P0 each round gives the safe sequence **P1 P3 P0 P2 P4**. (Other safe sequences exist; the textbook often shows P1 P3 P4 P0 P2.)

**Safe** means there is at least one order in which everyone can finish. **Unsafe** does not always mean deadlock, but deadlock becomes possible.

## Livelock and starvation

- **Livelock**: threads keep reacting to each other without progress.
- **Starvation**: a thread never gets the resource (unfair locks).

quiz.q: Why does `count++` from two threads lose updates?
options: It is a load-add-store sequence that can interleave
quiz.explain: Interleaved read-modify-write steps cause lost updates.

quiz.q: Which is a simple, practical way to prevent deadlocks?
options: Always acquire locks in the same global order
quiz.explain: A global lock order breaks circular wait.

quiz.q: In the Banker's algorithm, Need equals...
quiz.explain: Need is what a process may still request.

exercise.title: Banker's algorithm: is the state safe?
exercise.prompt:
Implement the **Banker's safety algorithm**.

**Input**:
- `n m` - number of processes (1 to 50) and resource types (1 to 10)
- one line with `m` numbers: **Available**
- `n` lines with `m` numbers: **Max** for P0..P(n-1)
- `n` lines with `m` numbers: **Allocation** for P0..P(n-1)

**Algorithm**: `Need = Max - Allocation`, `Work = Available`. Repeat: scan from **P0 upward** and choose the **first** unfinished process with `Need <= Work` for every resource; mark it finished and add its Allocation to Work. Then start the next scan from P0 again.

**Output**: if all processes finish, print `SAFE:` followed by the sequence, e.g. `SAFE: P1 P3 P0 P2 P4`. Otherwise print `UNSAFE`.

Example input:
```
3 1
1
5
4
2
2
2
1
```
Output:
```
SAFE: P2 P1 P0
```

tests.output: SAFE: P1 P3 P0 P2 P4

lessons.title: The command line: Windows, Linux and macOS
lessons.summary: Use the shell to navigate, manage files and processes on all three major systems.

slides.title: What is a shell?
slides.text:
A **shell** reads your commands and asks the OS to run them.

- Windows: **PowerShell** (and old `cmd`), in **Windows Terminal**
- macOS: **zsh** (default) in Terminal
- Linux: usually **bash** (also zsh, fish)
slides.narration: A shell is a program that reads the commands you type and asks the operating system to run them. On Windows the modern shell is PowerShell, inside Windows Terminal. On macOS the default is zsh, and on most Linux systems it is bash.

slides.title: Moving around
slides.text:
| Task | Linux / macOS | PowerShell |
|---|---|---|
| where am I | `pwd` | `pwd` / `Get-Location` |
| list | `ls -la` | `ls` / `Get-ChildItem` |
| change dir | `cd docs` | `cd docs` |
| make dir | `mkdir src` | `mkdir src` |
slides.narration: The basic navigation commands are almost the same everywhere. P w d prints where you are, l s lists files, c d changes directory, and m k dir makes a new folder. PowerShell provides these short names as aliases for its longer commands.

slides.title: Files
slides.text:
| Task | Linux / macOS | PowerShell |
|---|---|---|
| copy | `cp a b` | `cp a b` / `Copy-Item` |
| move | `mv a b` | `mv a b` / `Move-Item` |
| delete | `rm a` | `rm a` / `Remove-Item` |
| show | `cat a` | `cat a` / `Get-Content` |
| search text | `grep word a` | `Select-String word a` |
slides.narration: For files, copy, move, remove and show have similar names too. To search inside files, Linux and macOS use grep, while PowerShell uses Select String. Be careful with remove: there is no recycle bin on the command line.

slides.title: Processes from the shell
slides.text: Linux / macOS and PowerShell:
slides.narration: You can also manage processes from the shell. On Linux and macOS, p s lists processes, top shows a live view, and kill stops one by its ID. In PowerShell, Get Process and Stop Process do the same jobs.
slides.code:
# Linux / macOS
ps aux | grep python
top            # live view (q to quit)
kill 4242      # ask process 4242 to stop

# PowerShell
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5
Stop-Process -Id 4242

slides.title: Pipes and redirection
slides.text:
- `|` sends one command's output into another
- `>` writes output to a file, `>>` appends
- `<` reads input from a file

`./myprog < input.txt > output.txt`
slides.narration: Shells let you connect programs. The pipe symbol sends the output of one command into the next. The greater than sign saves output to a file, and the less than sign feeds a file as input. This is exactly how you can test a C program with a prepared input file.

slides.title: Compiling and running C
slides.text:
```
# Linux / macOS (gcc or clang)
gcc -Wall -O2 main.c -o main
./main < input.txt

# Windows (MSVC Developer PowerShell)
cl /W4 main.c
.\main.exe
```
The current folder is not in PATH: use `./` or `.\`.
slides.narration: To compile a C program from the command line, use gcc or clang on Linux and macOS, or the Microsoft compiler on Windows. Then run the program with dot slash on Unix systems, or dot backslash on Windows, because the current folder is not searched automatically for security reasons.

lessons.notes:
## Shells and terminals

- **Terminal** = the window (Windows Terminal, macOS Terminal, iTerm2, GNOME Terminal).
- **Shell** = the program interpreting commands: **bash**, **zsh** (macOS default since 2019), **fish**, **PowerShell 7** (cross-platform), `cmd.exe` (legacy).
- Windows 11 also offers **WSL** (Windows Subsystem for Linux) to run a real Linux userland, and a built-in `sudo` command.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | bash / zsh | PowerShell |
|---|---|---|
| current folder | `pwd` | `Get-Location` (`pwd`) |
| list files | `ls -la` | `Get-ChildItem` (`ls`, `dir`) |
| change folder | `cd ~/code` | `cd $HOME\code` |
| create folder | `mkdir -p a/b` | `New-Item -ItemType Directory a\b` |
| copy / move / delete | `cp`, `mv`, `rm -r` | `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Remove-Item -Recurse` |
| view file | `cat`, `less` | `Get-Content` |
| find text | `grep -rn "TODO" .` | `Select-String -Path *.c -Pattern TODO` |
| processes | `ps aux`, `top`, `kill PID` | `Get-Process`, `Stop-Process -Id PID` |
| environment var | `echo $PATH`, `export X=1` | `$env:PATH`, `$env:X = 1` |
| help | `man ls`, `ls --help` | `Get-Help Get-ChildItem` |

## Pipes and redirection

```bash
ls -l | sort -k5 -n | tail -3    # three largest files
./scheduler < tests/in1.txt > out.txt
diff out.txt tests/out1.txt      # compare with expected
```

PowerShell pipes **objects**, not plain text, which makes filtering easier: `Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 10`.

## PATH

The `PATH` variable lists folders searched for commands. The current folder is not included by default on Unix, so run local programs as `./main` (PowerShell: `.\main.exe`).

## Safety tips

- `rm -rf` and `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force` delete without a recycle bin.
- Read a command before pasting it from the internet.
- Use `sudo` (Linux/macOS/Windows 11) only when needed.
- Tab completion and the up arrow save lots of typing.

quiz.q: What is the default shell on modern macOS?
quiz.explain: macOS switched from bash to zsh in 2019 (Catalina).

quiz.q: What does `./prog < in.txt > out.txt` do?
options: Runs prog reading stdin from in.txt and writing stdout to out.txt
quiz.explain: < redirects input, > redirects output.

quiz.q: Which PowerShell command lists processes?
quiz.explain: Get-Process returns process objects.

lessons.task: In your terminal: create a folder `os-lab`, inside it create `notes.txt` with three lines, list the folder, search for a word in the file, copy the file, rename the copy, and delete it. Then list the 5 processes using the most CPU. Write down every command you used, on your own OS.

lessons.title: Security, users and permissions
lessons.summary: Learn how the OS protects users and files with accounts, permissions, and least privilege, and decode Unix permission modes in C.

slides.title: Who are you?
slides.text:
The OS keeps track of **users** and **groups**.

- Every process runs **as** a user
- **Authentication**: prove identity (password, passkey, biometrics)
- **Authorization**: what you may do
slides.narration: Operating systems know about users and groups, and every process runs as some user. Authentication is proving who you are, with a password, a passkey or a fingerprint. Authorization decides what you are then allowed to do.

slides.title: Unix permissions
slides.text:
`-rwxr-xr-- 1 ana dev 812 notes.sh`

- three sets: **owner**, **group**, **others**
- each: **r**ead, **w**rite, e**x**ecute
- octal: r=4, w=2, x=1 -> `rwxr-xr--` = **754**
slides.narration: On Linux and macOS each file has three sets of permissions: for the owner, for the group, and for everyone else. Each set has read, write and execute. In octal, read is four, write is two and execute is one, so r w x r dash x r dash dash becomes seven five four.

slides.title: Changing permissions
slides.text: Common commands:
slides.narration: You change permissions with chmod, using either octal numbers or letters. Seven five five is typical for programs and folders, six four four for normal files, and six hundred for private files like SSH keys. Chown changes the owner.
slides.code:
chmod 755 deploy.sh      # rwxr-xr-x
chmod 644 index.html     # rw-r--r--
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
chmod u+x script.sh      # add execute for owner
sudo chown ana:dev report.txt
ls -l

slides.title: Windows: ACLs and UAC
slides.text:
- NTFS uses **ACLs**: lists of allow/deny entries per user or group
- **UAC**: even admins run with standard rights until they approve elevation
- `icacls file` shows permissions
slides.narration: Windows uses access control lists. Each file has a list of entries that allow or deny specific users and groups. User Account Control means even administrators normally run with standard rights, and must approve before a program gets full power.

slides.title: Least privilege
slides.text:
- Don't use root/admin for daily work
- `sudo` only for single commands
- Services run as dedicated low-privilege users
- Sandboxing: apps on macOS, iOS, Android; containers on servers
slides.narration: The key security principle is least privilege: every user and program should have only the rights it needs. Do not work as root or administrator every day. Run services as special low privilege users. Modern systems also sandbox apps so they can only reach what they have been allowed.

slides.title: OS security features
slides.text:
- **ASLR**, non-executable memory (NX/DEP)
- **Secure Boot**, TPM, full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS)
- Automatic updates: **patch quickly**
- SELinux / AppArmor (Linux), Gatekeeper and SIP (macOS), Defender (Windows)
slides.narration: Modern systems have many built in protections: random memory layouts, memory that cannot be executed, secure boot with a TPM chip, and full disk encryption like BitLocker, FileVault and LUKS. The most important habit of all is simple: install security updates quickly.

lessons.notes:
## Users, groups, processes

Each account has a user ID (UID on Unix, SID on Windows) and belongs to groups. Every process carries the identity of the user who started it, and the kernel checks that identity on every protected operation (open a file, kill a process, bind port 80).

- **root** (UID 0) on Unix and **Administrator/SYSTEM** on Windows have broad power.
- **Authentication** - proving identity: passwords, **passkeys**, biometrics, hardware keys.
- **Authorization** - checking permissions.

## Unix permission bits

```
-rwxr-x---  1 ana  dev  812  Mar 3  build.sh
 \_/\_/\_/
 owner group others
```

| Symbol | Octal | File meaning | Directory meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| r | 4 | read contents | list names |
| w | 2 | modify | create/delete entries |
| x | 1 | execute | enter (`cd`) |

`rwxr-x---` = 7,5,0 = **750**. Common modes: 755 (programs, folders), 644 (files), 600 (private keys).

```bash
chmod 640 config.yml
chmod g+w shared.txt
umask 022          # default: new files 644, folders 755
```

Special bits: **setuid** (run as file owner, e.g. `passwd`), setgid, **sticky** bit on `/tmp`.

## Windows

- NTFS **ACLs** with allow/deny entries (Read, Write, Modify, Full control); inheritance from folders.
- `icacls C:\data` to view or change.
- **UAC** prompts before elevation; Windows 11 adds an optional `sudo` command.

## Least privilege and isolation

- Daily work as a normal user; elevate per command.
- Services under dedicated accounts (`www-data`, `nginx`, `LocalService`).
- Sandboxes: mobile app permissions, macOS App Sandbox, browser sandboxes, containers with namespaces and cgroups, seccomp.
- **Mandatory access control**: SELinux, AppArmor.

## Defense in depth

ASLR, NX/DEP, stack canaries, Secure Boot, TPM, disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS), firewalls, signed drivers, and above all **timely updates**. Most real attacks exploit known, already-patched bugs.

quiz.q: What does chmod 644 give?
What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give users and programs only the rights they need
quiz.explain: Minimal rights limit damage from mistakes and attacks.

quiz.q: On a directory, what does the x (execute) permission allow?
options: Entering it and accessing items inside
quiz.explain: For directories, x means you can traverse/enter it.

exercise.title: Decode permission modes
exercise.prompt:
Convert Unix octal permission modes into `rwx` strings.

**Input**: several lines, each a 3-digit octal mode (each digit 0-7) for owner, group and others. Read until end of input.

**Output**: for each mode print the mode, a space, and 9 characters: for each digit, `r` if it includes 4, `w` if it includes 2, `x` if it includes 1, otherwise `-`.

Example input:
```
755
640
```
Output:
```
755 rwxr-xr-x
640 rw-r-----
```
